title: 2026 Is the Year of Return: Models Have No Secrets, Applications Have Moats
dek: Model capability progress is slowing, Chinese open-source models have compressed the gap to 6-12 months, and the API business has no monopolistic barrier; what's truly valuable is the layer of context, tools and environment outside the model.
why: ZhenFund's Dai Yusen breaks down 2026 with three R's (Return, Research, Remember), and his second-half commentary on OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Manus one by one is bolder than the main episode.
who: Investors watching the pace of AI primary-market bets, AI application founders choosing a direction, and engineers who want to understand the moat debate around model companies.
skip: After 2:36 the chit-chat can be skipped; just listen to the four segments on OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Manus, the rest of the commentary is scattered.

points.h: The AI commercialization chain was validated this year
points.body: At the end of last year, Yusen's analogy was: AI is still learning fast, it's a very smart elementary school student, but an elementary school student going to work probably can't earn money yet, so we first need to see technological progress, then that progress landing in products, and only then commercialization. In 2025 this chain was validated: ChatGPT revenue grew very fast, Anthropic's API grew very fast, Coding applications like Cursor and Cloud Code reached close to $1 billion ARR, and Agent applications like Manus and GenSpark are heading toward $100 million ARR. At the start of the year he judged that reasoning ability, coding ability and Computer Use together would unlock the year of the Agent, and this year we indeed saw L3-level Coding Agents that can program on their own for over an hour, as well as general-purpose Agent products.

points.h: Chinese models have compressed the gap to 6 to 12 months
points.body: At the start of the year everyone worried Chinese companies lacked cards and talent and would lag for a long time. After DeepSeek burst onto the scene, everyone found you could catch up to near the world frontier at one-tenth the cost or even less; later Chain One, Kimi K2, GLM, MiniMax and a series of ByteDance models could all, a few months after a US SOTA release, put out open-source models with close performance at one-fifth to one-tenth the cost. At the start of the year the open-source ecosystem was still dominated by Llama, now it's basically Chinese models' world, and even Cursor's Composer 1 is widely believed to be trained on Chinese open-source models. Yusen thinks completely surpassing them in the short term is very hard, but narrowing the gap to 6 to 12 months is fairly realistic.

points.h: Models have no secrets, and API is not a monopoly business
points.body: Yusen says information and talent flow very fast in this industry, especially in Silicon Valley where there are no non-competes, so a lot of know-how can't be fully kept secret, plus everyone has hundreds of thousands of cards and the data is roughly similar, so it's hard to open up a generational gap. He gives the example of Manus: at launch it was originally all Claude 3.7 APIs, because at the time only it could run Agentic products, but soon they found Gemini also ran well and was cheaper, so they switched a large volume to Gemini; later Codex launched and its coding ability was also strong. For an API user, switching between models is easy, and application companies can instead draw on the strengths of many and use the best model for different tasks — which precisely shows that selling APIs itself has a low barrier and is not a monopolistic business.

points.h: Applications go from sashimi to a Manchu Han feast to have a moat
points.body: The first batch of AI applications in 2023 mostly just made an external UI for the model; users interacted with the model through the UI and what they got was still the model's output. Yusen's analogy was ‘sashimi, which is fish plus wasabi and soy sauce’. Complex applications now are different: they need the user's own context, industry-specific data, and the history of the user's interaction with the application (memory), which the model itself doesn't have; at the same time the Agent can use more tools and change its environment, for example writing a piece of code for itself to use. So outside the model layer there's an extra context layer, and an environment-and-tools layer, and the analogy goes from sashimi to a Manchu Han feast — ingredient quality still matters, but service, environment and cooking skill matter too. Manus beat all advanced models on the Remote Labor Index test released by Scale, precisely because it really does more things on top of the model.

points.h: 2026 is the Year of R, and the first R is Return
points.body: Over the past few years everyone bet on AI investment continuing to exceed expectations, drawn by the potential for big returns. But now the investment is getting bigger and bigger, and about 50% of the investment in data centers is compute, and these cards may become obsolete after 4 to 6 years, so investment needs to see results within a shorter return cycle. At the same time marginal returns on the model side are declining: the progress of GPT-5 over GPT-4 is not as big as GPT-4 over GPT-3, while the investment is much larger, and it still can't stop Chinese open-source models from approaching at low cost and fast speed. On the application side last year was low expectations and high growth, now everyone is very optimistic about 26 and 27, and expectations are already very high. The $20 billion question raised by Sequoia's David later became the $60 billion question, and now this account is getting harder and harder to figure out.

points.h: The second R is Research, the third R is Remember
points.body: Yusen says AI history has always been a process of scaling and research alternating, and now it's again time for research to improve, and Demis also believes one to two research breakthroughs are still needed to reach AGI. Silicon Valley therefore has a new trend of investing in New Labs — opportunities centered on researchers exploring differentiation from top model companies, such as Thinking Machines, Ilya's SSI, Reflections, Human End, these new research labs that start at $1 billion valuations. The third R is Remember/Memory: without memory, the result you get asking AI and I get asking AI are the same; now ChatGPT's understanding of him is already much higher than a new chatbot's, because there are three years of chat records. But current memory is basically still retrieval-based, like a friend relying on a very thick notebook to record every sentence, rather than truly understanding you at the model weight level.

points.h: The bubble hasn't peaked, but long-end expectations may turn pessimistic
points.body: Yusen thinks every technological revolution in human history has brought a bubble, and it's quite natural that AI may bring the biggest bubble in human history. But we haven't reached the top of the bubble yet, because the top of a bubble shows asset prices absurdly high, even bad companies and fraudulent companies very high, while currently Nvidia and these companies' short-term valuations are even very low. What he really worries about is the change in long-end expectations: now the short end is still very optimistic about Nvidia's expectations for next year and the year after, but if the long end turns pessimistic about the AI landing return cycle getting longer and AGI arrival slowing, then no matter how good short-end performance is it won't be the main trading factor. He judges that next year US stocks may see a fairly obvious pullback, the timing possibly in the second half, and OpenAI's own user and revenue growth will be an important trigger.

points.h: When intelligence gets cheap, agency and taste become valuable
points.body: Yusen says intelligence has always been a luxury in human history; those who can mobilize smart people at scale are either top enterprises or national governments. Now $20 buys a lot of intelligence, so first, execution becomes cheap, because AI can help you execute and write code, and what matters is agency and taste — what you want to do, whether you have something you want to do yourself, and which of the three methods AI gives you you choose. Second, we used to do things linearly, first A then B then C, now we can complete many things in parallel; programming with AI is giving different agents different tasks and being responsible for giving instructions yourself, you have to be a good boss to AI. Third, use the most advanced tools more to experience the future; those who used ChatGPT earliest may thereby have a more optimistic judgment about AI.

quotes.text: AI is still learning fast, it's a very smart elementary school student, but an elementary school student going to work probably can't earn money yet, so we first need to see technological progress, then that progress landing in products, and only then commercialization.
If you replace a lot of programmers, it doesn't mean you can earn those programmers' salaries, it means the tasks those programmers used to complete have become worthless.

It's like your friend's understanding of you comes entirely from a very thick notebook recording every sentence of your chats, whereas true memory is certainly that he doesn't need to carry this notebook, he already understands you more deeply inside.
When everyone is very optimistic, prepare for pessimism; when everyone is very pessimistic, prepare for optimism. I think that's a contrarian way of thinking.
Don't define yourself with the product form of the previous era. Right, I think don't call it AI's so-and-so, so-and-so is a product form of the previous era.
